speaker: Swami Sivananda
title: Moderation and discipline in diet (Mitahara)
text: Take Sattvic food. Give up chillies, tamarind, garlic, onion, sour articles, oil, mustard, asafoetida. Observe moderation in diet (Mitahara). Do not overload the stomach. Give up those things which the mind likes best for a fortnight once or twice in a year. Eat simple food. Milk and fruits help concentration. Take food as medicine to keep the life going. Eating for enjoyment is a sin. Give up salt and sugar for a week or a fortnight. You must be able to live on rice, dhal and bread without any pickle. Do not ask for extra salt for dhal, and sugar for tea, coffee and milk. People taking non-vegetarian diet should try their best to gradually give up flesh-eating as completely as possible. They will be immensely benefited.
modern_interpretation: This timeless wisdom encourages mindful eating, seeing food as essential fuel rather than purely for pleasure. It's about developing strong self-control over cravings and practicing regular 'detoxes' from beloved but potentially distracting foods (like a digital detox for your diet) to sharpen your willpower and focus. By simplifying your diet and prioritizing foods that promote mental clarity, you cultivate inner discipline and create space for deeper concentration, ultimately enhancing overall well-being and spiritual growth.
summary: Swami Sivananda advocates for a Sattvic, moderate diet (Mitahara), emphasizing food as medicine for sustenance rather than indulgence, and encourages periodic fasting from preferred tastes and a gradual transition away from non-vegetarianism to cultivate discipline and enhance concentration.
actionable_advice: Identify one food item or taste you crave most and consciously abstain from it for a short, set period (e.g., a week or fortnight) to practice self-control and observe your mind's reactions without judgment.
embedding_ready_text: This teaching from Swami Sivananda on diet emphasizes profound self-discipline and detachment, advocating for Sattvic, moderate eating (Mitahara) and treating food as medicine, not pleasure. It directly addresses emotional states like craving, indulgence, and lack of focus, guiding individuals away from unhealthy habits and attachment to sensory gratification. By encouraging periodic fasting from favored foods and a gradual shift from non-vegetarianism, it aims to enhance mental clarity, willpower, and inner peace, offering a transformative path to improved self-control and spiritual purity. This wisdom is crucial for anyone struggling with impulse control, seeking greater focus, or aiming to cultivate a more disciplined and mindful approach to consumption.
